message.content:
The smell hit me first, thick and wrong, like burnt copper and wet wool. It wasn't the clean ozone of a standard fault; this was the scent of something organic being ground into the metal. My boots clicked on the slick grating as the belt roared closer, the heat radiating against my skin, the line stopping just inches from my grasp. The companion stood on the wrong side of the moving metal, their face twisted in a silent scream that I could not hear.

I had to act fast, but my movements felt slow, heavy with the weight of a failing system. I lunged forward, grabbing the edge of the moving chain, but the friction burned my palms raw. I yanked hard, trying to pull them back, but the metal held firm, unyielding. The rescue failed instantly. There was no time to hesitate, no room for a second attempt. The belt surged forward, swallowing the gap between us, and I was left holding only the cold, slick edge of the machine.

I tried to stop the machine, to break the loop, but the logic was too strong. The gears were grinding harder than ever, the metal shrieking against itself as the companion's body twisted, caught in the loops and cycles. I could not force the machine to see the truth, to make it understand that some things could not be sorted, only stopped. The gears spun on, indifferent to the life trapped inside the casing.

I stood there, trapped in the wrong side of the machinery, waiting for the line stop. There was no escape, no signal to send, no way to intervene. The only evidence of what had happened was the smell, the sound of the hum, and the fact that the companion was gone. The stakes were high, the danger real, and the only thing left was the silence of a failed attempt. I was left with the memory of the touch, the cold hand, and the knowledge that I had failed to stop it. The smell remained, the only proof that something had gone terribly wrong.
